title: Cable selection
summary: Shows how to select a cable size using design current, protective device rating, correction factors, current carrying capacity and voltage drop, with a worked shower circuit example.

sections.heading: What decides cable size
paragraphs: Cable size depends on the current rating under defined installation conditions, the maximum permitted voltage drop (BS 7671 Section 525, values in Appendix 4, section 6.4) and meeting earth fault loop impedance requirements in Tables 41.2, 41.3 and 41.4.
bullets: Design current, Ib: the cable must carry the full load current
Type of cable: PVC, MIMS, copper or aluminium conductors
Installed conditions, e.g. clipped to a surface or with other cables in trunking
Surrounding temperature: resistance rises as temperature rises and insulation may melt
Type and size of protection: how long the cable carries fault current

sections.heading: Current carrying capacity and steps
paragraphs: To comply with BS 7671, Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz must hold, and It ≥ Iz. Ib is the design current of the circuit, In the rated current or setting of the protective device, Iz the current carrying capacity of a cable for continuous service under the installation conditions, and It the tabulated current carrying capacity.

Steps: find the design current Ib after any diversity; select the protective device with In equal to or larger than Ib; determine and apply the correction factors; determine the installation method; and select the cable from the current carrying capacity tables in Appendix 4.
bullets: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz and It ≥ Iz

sections.heading: Correction factors
paragraphs: Several correction factors take installation conditions into account.
bullets: Cc: buried in ground or duct in ground = 0.9; above ground = 1
Cf: semi-enclosed fuse to BS 3036 = 0.725, otherwise 1
Ci: thermal insulation (Regulation 523.9): tabulated if in contact with a thermally conductive surface on one side; 0.5 if totally surrounded over more than 0.5 m; for less than 0.5 m use Table 52.2
Cs: thermal resistivity of soil, Table 4B3

sections.heading: Worked example: semi-enclosed fuse
paragraphs: Example 1: a 6.5 kW, 230 V shower, 18 m from the consumer unit, flat twin with cpc clipped to ceiling joists with one other cable, roof space 35°C, insulation up to the top of the joists, TN-S supply. Ib = 6,500 ÷ 230 = 28.26 A. A BS 3036 semi-enclosed fuse gives In = 30 A.

Factors: Ca = 0.94, Cc = 1, Cf = 0.725, Cg = 0.8. Iz = 30 ÷ (0.94 ✕ 1 ✕ 0.725 ✕ 0.8) = 55 A. Reference Method 100, Table 4D5 column 2: 16 mm² (It = 57 A). Voltage drop = 2.8 ✕ 10-3 ✕ 28.26 ✕ 18 = 1.42 V, less than the 11.5 V maximum (5% of 230 V), so 16 mm² is chosen.
bullets: Maximum volt drop: 5% of nominal supply voltage = 11.5 V
16 mm² gives 2.8 mV per ampere metre

sections.heading: Worked example: Type B circuit breaker
paragraphs: With a Type B CB to BS EN 60898, In = 32 A (next size up from 28.26 A) and Cf = 1. Iz = 32 ÷ (0.94 ✕ 1 ✕ 1 ✕ 0.8) = 42.6 A. From Table 4D5 column 2, 10 mm² (It = 45 A) is required.
Voltage drop = 4.4 ✕ 10-3 ✕ 28.26 ✕ 18 = 2.24 V, below 11.5 V, so 10 mm² is chosen when circuit breaker protection is used.
bullets: 10 mm² gives 4.4 mV per ampere metre

flashcards.front: Name three things cable size depends on.
flashcards.back: Current rating under installation conditions, the maximum permitted voltage drop (Section 525), and earth fault loop impedance requirements (Tables 41.2, 41.3, 41.4).
The full load current the cable must carry, found after applying any diversity.
Cable resistance increases as temperature increases, and insulation may melt if it is too high.

flashcards.back: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, and It ≥ Iz.
The current carrying capacity of a cable for continuous service under the particular installation conditions.
The rated current or current setting of the protective device.
The ambient or surrounding temperature correction factor (Tables 4B1 and 4B2).
0.725 for a semi-enclosed fuse to BS 3036, otherwise 1.
The grouping correction factor, from Tables 4C1 to 4C6.
